title: File Handling
summary: Read and write files safely using Python's with statement.

checkpoints.title: Opening files with `with`
checkpoints.content: `with open("notes.txt") as f:` opens a file and guarantees it gets closed automatically when the block ends, even if an error happens inside. Inside the block, `f.read()` returns the whole file as one string, and `f.readlines()` returns a list of lines.
checkpoints.explanation: Using `with` instead of a bare `open()`/`close()` pair avoids the classic bug of forgetting to close a file, which can leak resources or leave writes unflushed to disk.

hints.H0: `with` sets up automatic cleanup for you.
hints.H1: The file is guaranteed to close when the indented block ends.
hints.H2: f.read() gets the whole file as a string; f.readlines() gets a list of lines.

checkpoints.title: Predict what happens after the with block
checkpoints.content: After `with open("data.txt") as f: contents = f.read()` finishes, what is true about f?

options.text: f is automatically closed — trying to read from it again would raise an error.
options.explanation: The with statement closes the file the moment its indented block ends, whether it finished normally or raised an exception.

options.text: f stays open until the program exits, so you can keep reading from it.
options.explanation: That would be true of a bare open() without with — the whole point of with is closing it immediately when the block ends.

options.text: The file data.txt is deleted from disk.
options.explanation: Reading and closing a file never deletes it — that would require an explicit os.remove() call.

checkpoints.explanation: The with statement's whole purpose is guaranteed, automatic cleanup — the file handle closes as soon as the block exits.

hints.H0: with is specifically designed around automatic cleanup.
hints.H1: That cleanup means closing the file the moment the block ends.
hints.H2: f is closed — further reads on it would fail.

checkpoints.title: Open a file for writing
checkpoints.content: Write the with statement that opens "log.txt" for writing (not reading) and binds it to the name f.
checkpoints.explanation: The second argument to open() is the mode — "w" opens for writing, creating the file if needed or overwriting it if it already exists.

hints.H0: open() takes a second argument controlling read vs write mode.
hints.H1: The mode string for writing is a single letter.

checkpoints.title: Choose the append mode
checkpoints.content: Which mode string opens a file so new writes are added to the end, without erasing what's already there?

options.explanation: "a" (append) opens the file for writing but starts at the end, preserving existing content instead of overwriting it.
"w" (write) truncates the file first — anything already in it is erased before your new writes go in.
"r" (read) opens the file read-only — attempting to write would raise an error.

checkpoints.explanation: "a" is the append mode — it's the one mode that adds to existing content instead of replacing or merely reading it.

hints.H0: Three common modes are read, write, and append.
hints.H1: Only one of them preserves existing content while still allowing writes.
